10 Archetypes Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/10-archetypes/10-archetypes-transcript

                                                                        May 11, 2019

This is session ten of the audio series and it’s entitled “The 6 archetypes of drama”.
Something to keep in mind as you study these archetypes: there’s nothing more to do
with them once you find them, but to observe them and notice, and be aware, and then
practice acceptance that we talked about in the previous session.

The critical element of this process is to stay in the point of view of awareness and
witness, and observation, because if you try and go fix what you find, you’ll find that
that “fix it” is based in a reaction, and that reaction “to fix it” is based in a
 prior reaction of feeling victimized or finding something wrong with, which is a
judgment of what you’ve come to observe.

So all our “fix it” and “change it” modalities are just another reaction,
and what we’re really endeavoring to do is to suspend and to refrain from
those reactions. Even if the story in our mind says we should fix it, we
should change it, what we’ll endeavor to do is to be an Observer of that
story also and watch its characters and point of view.

So all our “fix it” and “change it” modalities are just another reaction, and what we’re
really endeavoring to do is to suspend and to refrain from those reactions. Even if the
story in our mind says we should fix it, we should change it, what we’ll endeavor to do is
to be an Observer of that story also and watch its characters and point of view. So, all
you have to do is be aware and hold your center in your point of view and observe,
because as long as you’re there, you’re no longer living as one of these archetype
characters of reaction that so often take us into drama.

Today’s topic is about point of view, and we’ve talked about it a couple times before, and
I’ve given you an assignment to investigate and start to observe that. And today we’re
going to take it further. Those previous assignments were to prepare you for this leap. I
used to teach this course in a weekend, and what I found out is very few people could
digest and integrate all the information to make it really useful: it might make sense to
them, they might understand it, but they weren’t necessarily able to use it, to really
dissect their stories, their dreams, their points of view and dissolve their agreements.
That’s why I’ve given these assignments about point of view over a little longer time
period, so that you have time to shift your point of view and see it more clearly, and that
way it’s a lot more effective in dissolving agreements.

(1) The first assignment I gave you about your point of view was your attention (“The
Attention” session): to hunt your attention, to find out where it goes and what it gets
hooked by, but also to notice the point of view you’re perceiving it from. (2) The next
assignment along that avenue was to look at that point of view and start do describe it in
terms of aspects of your personality (“The Characters” session). We can also call them
                                                                                                                           1/10

“Masks that we wear” or “Archetypes” – it’s the word that I typically use. A couple of
common ones that I gave you were the Judge and the Victim, and I allowed you to come
up with all the others that you could find about yourself. I gave you that latitude because
there’s neither right or wrong way to do it, but it’s however you see yourself – whatever
you find is perfect for you. Don’t expect that we’ll see ourselves perfectly, clearly and
with a full understanding of all our points of view and all our personalities in the first
month of this.

This assignment is specifically about archetypes, and those two previous assignments
were to prepare you for this one. While the other ones that you may have come up with
are wonderful and helpful, they are not right or wrong, they are not good or bad, they
are great, these specific 6 are the ones that we portray, we create, we live out. They are
the ones that create the most drama in our lives. And if this is about being happy in our
lives, and this is about living with peace of mind, then this is about eliminating conflict
and these 6 archetypes are all about creating conflict.

Let me talk about the six characters that we are going to focus on:

The first – the Judge. It’s a big primary voice in many of our heads, and it is always
comparing. Its basic function, the core of it, is to compare, and it picks a side: we are
either on the side of “worse than” or “better than”, or something we do is better than
someone else does, or something we do is worse than someone else does. That
comparison generally relates to our self-worth. The other place that the Judge makes
a comparison is from a standard that’s set in our imagination. If we make a self-
judgment, comparing what we actually did with what we should have done, then what
we should have done is based on an imaginary character of ourselves, an image of
perfection, of “had we known better, we would have done this”. Well, that person that
we are imagining we should be doesn’t exist, never did, never will, but the Judge in our
mind is comparing us to this imaginary version of ourselves. It’s a little tough to
measure up when it’s not practical and realistic. We also create these imaginary versions
of other people: what other people should have done, what the world, the
environment, the policy or law should be – these are all versions that we hold in our
imagination that the Judge in our mind then compares the world to, or other people to,
and finds something wrong with the world, based on this imagined version. Well, let’s
go back and really suspend our judgment, and notice that the world is the way the
world is – and we’re back to acceptance.

And this could be very subtle, and it can start as an observation of comparison, and
then start to distort into a self-worth arrangement. I had a very interesting experience
along these lines. It was a number of years back, and I was teaching with another
teacher. She was quite wonderful, really enjoyed spending time with her, and then we
were kind of trading off of what we were doing during the week, and she led this group
into an exercise, and she did it quite beautifully, quite masterfully, and I was very
impressed, and just was commenting to myself: “Wow, she did that really well, she is
really great.” And it was just an appreciation. And then that idea started to go to “She


                                                                                                                           2/10

did that better than I would have done that,” and it was still just a comparison, it was an
honest assessment, it was like “She did really well,” “It’s a piece of work that she’s really
good at,” and then the next level of the iteration went into “I won’t be able to do it that
well,” which then went into “I wish I was as good as her,” – that’s where the judgment
hit. It went from that desire to do something that well to “I don’t do it as well as her,
and because of that I’m not as good as her,” – it’s a very subtle shift between
comparison to judgment, cause we can compare without implying any value or any
meaning to our self-worth. I can look at her work, as I did initially, and say “Gosh, she
did it really great,” and by that to inspire myself to want to be that good at something, to
see a new level of mastery and say “Ok, I really want to do it that way. ”But the moment
I went into the judgment was when just the attitude shifted. I even could have had the
same words and said “I want to do it that way,” as a comparison, as a desire, but then
they would end to “I want to do it that way,” which is just a shift in the tone, a shift in
the attitude of “I wish I could do it that way,” and now it’s about me being not good
enough. The subtlety was just in the tone, in the attitude of the words I was saying. You
see, in my mind I had made the analysis, the comparison of the quality of mastery, and I
assumed, and my judgment assumed, that that meant something about my worth –
that’s how subtle the Judge can be. We can even say something that’s true, but with a
certain attitude we’d put ourselves down.

(2) Second archetype – the Victim. And the Victim often goes hand in hand with the
Judge. The Victim is the one that receives that agreement from the Judge and agrees
with it. It’s like you have one voice talking in your head that says: “She did that better
than me,” – “She’s better than me” is implied, and the Victim goes: “Yes, she is better
than me, I am worse than her,” – that is the agreement that the Victim makes. And a lot
of times, those Judge and Victim can speak together, and both of them can be speaking
at the same time with the same words – they come in as a duet and they go: “Oh, she’s
better than me,” and I get the judgment in that, putting myself down, and I get the
agreement in that comment. And they come from two different aspects of my
personality – the Victim and the Judge – at the same time, in the same sentence. And
now I’ve got two voices in my head saying the same thing and it looks even more true.
Part of what we’re going to do is split those apart, just by identifying those two as
specifically different. The Victim is classically identified as an attitude. And the attitude
is basically hopelessness, powerlessness, “The world is doing something
to me that I do not deserve, that I cannot control, and I am suffering
because what the world or someone else is doing to me.” The Victim is also
characterized by a lot of blame. One of the primary emotions that you will find with
victim-hood is fear. It’s the fear of not knowing, not being in control, not being safe.

These are two you’re probably already quite familiar with, and they are the two aspects
that we, in this society, have learned to play out a great deal. And they are so common,
they look like we are supposed to play them, like we’re perfectly rationalized and
justified in playing them. However the price of playing them is emotionally very high.





                                                                                                                           3/10

(3) Third character we are going to call the Hero. You may have come up with this
archetype of the Hero in your own study of yourself. The Hero, we can also call the Fixer
– person who has to make everything right, the Healer, the Teacher – these are all kind
of aspects of the Hero. They are the one that is going to rush in and make everything ok,
or at least there’s an aspect of the Hero pretty much in that attitude. Now, the Hero’s
primary motivator for rushing in and making things ok is to protect and save
themselves or others, and also to prove themselves worthy to do the good deed, so that
they are appreciated and rewarded, so that they get the attention and respect, and
acceptance of those that they have proven themselves worthy around. So often that
classic Hero image is the one that wins the race, the Performer that has done so well
that the crowd cheers for, that other people love. This is the reward that we’ve been
conditioned in society to get for being a top performer. And so often we get conditioned
to perform well. And we get conditioned to perform well, because we love the rewards,
because we love the attention, the accolades, the love, and we even go on performing
when the rewards are not there anymore. I know for myself: I worked endlessly hard 80
to 110 hours a week, hoping somebody would notice and say what a great guy I was.
That was my version of the Hero. It started out when I got gold stars earlier in school,
and then I got grades, and then I got into a college, and then I got to please my boss and
get good reviews, and deliver on schedules – those were my performance criteria, that
was my winning the race.

That was one version of a Hero. How much we help people? How much we help people
driven by the motivation to have other people notice? That’s also a part of the Hero.
Don’t get me wrong. There’s nothing wrong with helping people, but what is the
motivation and what is the attitude behind it? And what may help you find the attitude
behind that motivation is asking yourself how you feel if nobody notices. You may feel
like it was empty, or that you are unappreciated, and there’s a reaction because these
expectations we didn’t know exist didn’t get met: “Oh, no one noticed,” and now there’s
a down. There wasn’t a reward, so you feel less happy about the outcome. That tells us
that some of our motivation is driven by this need for attention, acceptance, approval,
respect. A lot of our motivation at the same time can be just because we love doing what
we are doing, we love helping people, we love serving – there is an intrinsic joy in there.
And at the same time that there can be an intrinsic joy from our integrity to be with
people and community, to love and serve them, there can also be a Hero aspect that’s in
play that has the need for attention. And it’s the part that sets up the emotional reaction.
So we can have a very authentic service self and at the same we can have a Hero in
service, playing in our mind, playing in our behavior. So this is where our discernment,
our assessment and clarity of having 2 motivators come in, and we can split them apart.

(4) Fourth character – I’m going to call it the Villain. The Villain has a couple different
shapes and forms. (a) The classic version is the Rebel, it’s “Don’t tell me what to do”,
fighting the system, going your own way, whatever the structure is of “we want to do it
different” attitude. That can be a Rebel, that can be just your own independent
thinking, but if there’s an emotional reaction behind it, we’re going to call it the Rebel.
And it may not serve us. That Rebel is going to sabotage our own happiness in a way

                                                                                                                           4/10

that it’s all too willing to create a conflict with other people and their systems. (b1)
Another aspect of the Villain is a Saboteur. The Saboteur has a tendency to sabotage our
own well being: that may our emotional happiness, that may be our financial success,
that may be our relationship. That Saboteur may be willing to throw away the whole
relationship just because of a minor incident. It blows things out of proportion. It
overreacts and says: “Fine, I don’t want to have anything to do with you ever again,”
over something that could be quite small. (b2) Another aspect of the Saboteur is that it
often destroys and damages by neglect. That character archetype will talk us into not
making a phone call, not making amends, not doing what needs to be done to take care
of the situation. That part of our personality will tend to dismiss things, blow things of,
until they fall into disarray and create chaos. That’s part of the Saboteur and it’s not
necessarily overt the way the Rebel side, the Destroyer does with the anger. It can be
much more just through neglect and though what some people call “passive aggressive”.
But the results are that you end up with un-nurtured situations, un-nurtured
relationships, and chaos and emotional reaction are what festers. Both of these: the
Rebel, the Saboteur – I put them under the heading of the Villain. The Villain’s principal
attitude is one of anger, resentment, frustration. It is “against”, it is fighting, and it’s
fighting with an attitude that’s emotionally pretty destructive. When it comes out it
brings its anger, it brings its resentment, and it does its best to inflict harm or
punishment on someone else. Our Judge may determine that someone deserves it, and
they should be punished, and it’s our Villain that takes it out on them.

To give you an idea of what this looks like: we may be driving down the road, someone
cuts us off in traffic, we go to fear, we feel vulnerable and powerless over these outside
forces, we are afraid for a moment, we have a scary scenario of us possibly having an
accident, and that’s a Victim projection. Then our Judge takes over the ball, looks at the
person that almost caused this event and concludes that they were wrong: they were
wrong, they screwed up, they made a mistake. And for making that mistake the Judge
authorizes the Villain to go inflict punishment on this person, because they deserve it,
and all our anger comes out of our mouth, we curse, we make a hand gesture, whatever
that is, and we express that venom, because the Judge has decided that that person
deserves it, and we unleash our Villain’s venom on them. And that’s all in order to
protect the Victim, which feels powerless. This is how they start working together. Now,
so often those reactions of the Villain come out before we even noticed the Victim and
the Judge. They happened at high speed. This is why I’ve given you a couple of weeks to
kind of get used to the idea, track them, see them, so that you get faster, so that you can
see the subtleties and the speed in which they operate.

(5) The fifth character for us to look at is the Princess. The Princess’s primary attitude is
entitlement. The Princess aspect of our personality feels entitled, as if it deserves
something: whether it’s earned or just by its birth right – we are owed. And that can be
something as simple as a parking space: we pull into a parking lot, we see a space, we’re
going for it, another car from another direction pulls in ahead of us. We may have a
judgment: “Hey, they shouldn’t have done that,” we may feel victimized: “They took
my space,” but that judgment is based on the assumption, on the expectation that we

                                                                                                                           5/10

had a right to that space. You see the Princess set up the expectation that we didn’t
even see, we had the Victim reaction, according to which something was taken away
from us, and the Judge then said: “They shouldn’t have done that.” But the Judge and
the Victim were preceded by this Princess’s expectation of entitlement. Without that,
without that expectation of entitlement that we didn’t even see, we wouldn’t have a
judgment and victim reaction. Where we find betrayal, where we find injustice, that
Princess aspect is the part of us that sets up all these criteria of what we deserve, what
we’re owed, that we then have reactions upon when these criteria aren’t met. And when
things do show up, when they happen the way our Princess aspect expects – the way we
believe we’re entitled according to the Princess – we don’t appreciate them very much,
we take them for granted: “Of course that would be mine”, “Of course I would have
that.” And so we may come to an experience of some great gift, and we lack the point of
view of great gratitude, and appreciation for what life is giving us. Then it’s wonderful to
have expectations, but in both aspects, whether it doesn’t show up, we have the
emotional reaction and it’s unpleasant, and if things do show up, they are taken for
granted and it lacks the emotional richness and gratitude, and appreciation for life and
people around us. Then the Princess is a real road block to real authentic happiness,
because it lives in the sense of entitlement and then it lives in the sense of taking things
for granted. And a lot of these things are assumptions we have that we are not aware of.
Do we see the Victim reaction of feeling like we lost something that belonged to us, or
the judgment of another person for taking it away?

I was talking to a client that was worked in a company, and they were letting a lot of
people go because many of the positions were overlapping, and she didn’t know if she
would loose her job or not, and she kept referring to it as “my job”, and I had to ask her
how it was “her” job, and she’s like “Well I’ve had it for twelve years,” and what I asked
her was whether she had a right to give it away, and she’s like “No, I couldn’t give it to
anybody else, it’s somebody else who does the hiring,” and I was like “If it’s not yours to
give it away, how it could be yours?”, “Is it something that you can take with you?” –
“No, it’s a job that belongs to the company.” But just by calling it “my” job, she had a
sense that it was hers, that it belonged to her, that she was then entitled to it, and that if
they let her go, then they were doing her a disservice, that they were somehow betraying
her, they were somehow not appreciating her. What she didn’t realize was that that job
was never hers – that job always belonged to the company and she had no rights to it.

It’s not common that we look at our jobs this way, that we look at our careers this way,
that we look at people in our life this way. People in our life and our relationships –
sometimes they come, sometimes they go. I know a gentleman whose wife was leaving
him, and he was upset, he kept referring to her as “my” wife, as if she belonged to him,
as if he was entitled to it, he’d work hard in the relationship, he’d somehow earned it.
That was a Princess aspect coming through very strong. He was entitled to maybe just a
second chance in the relationship. What he didn’t recognize was that she was entitled to
 her choice of what she did, he wasn’t entitled to choose for her what she did, she did
not have an obligation to give him a second chance or third, or eighteenth chance, or
whatever it was in her mind. What he was finally able to see is that he doesn’t have a

                                                                                                                           6/10

right to what someone else’s choices are. He can dissolve that Princess entitlement, and
his Victim is no longer in reaction, and his judgment of the situation is no longer as
strong, and his Villain, that is so angry at her and other people around that situation
that side with her, doesn’t have a place to go. Then in this we see how we go from
Princess to Victim (“The world is taking something away”), to judgment (“These people
do not operate the way they should, according to what my Princess says is fair and
entitled”), and because of that the Villain comes out and says: “I’m going to punish you
and get angry at you for not living according to the archetype of entitlement, that I
believe I deserve,” – that’s the way we went from Princess to anger. And we often go so
fast – we are in anger and we don’t know how we got there, we never saw the
entitlement expectations creep in or that maybe they were there for years.

(6) Sixth archetype – the Prostitute. The Prostitute is that part of ourselves that
negotiates away our own happiness. The Prostitute is the part of ourselves that
sacrifices our emotional integrity to get something very small. This doesn’t have to do
with sex. It could be completely gender neutral. The Prostitute can be part of an aspect
of a businessman: a businessman who works so hard trying to get approval from some
co-workers, or a boss, or a raise, or promotion, so they sacrifice a life they enjoy, become
a workaholic, give up their happiness in their personal life, in their relationships, and
are focused on getting approval from someone else. We’ll call it just an external
approval, opinion or raise. That can be a Prostitute. It’s the part of ourselves that works
so hard to please another, even when what we are doing isn’t pleasing and enjoyable to
ourselves. Certainly there are cases where we need to do things that are challenging or
maybe things we don’t want to do. We may have a job and it may not be a job we really
want to be in. But if that job, that work provides for a family, puts food on a table and
gives us a shelter of a home, then that’s a small price to pay for having such a great
reward as food and survival, and well-being, and home, and hot and cold running
water. Then you have a great comfort in your life for you and your family for what you
have to do 8, 10, 12 hours a day. But at a certain point it’s no longer about survival, it’s
no longer about taking care of your needs, and when it’s no longer the motivation of
what is best in a balanced, emotional quality and practical physical needs of a family, it
becomes about what someone thinks of us – now the Prostitute’s at play. And these are
subtle things to figure out. This takes a very discerning eye to see the difference of
whether my motivation is in the emotional well being of my livelihood and my family,
or whether my motivation is for approval, to see whether there’s a fear that I’m not good
enough, a need for acceptance from the outside, and whether there’s just the survival
instinct of taking care of ourselves and our family. And out of both of those motivators
we would go to work and perform at our job or our career. So we end up with the same
result, but how do we discern the distinct difference, the subtle distinct difference
between what is the corrupt motivator of fear, of not getting approval and what is just
the need to provide to ourselves and our family? Well, that can be subtle to find. Then
as we practice unearthing all these characters and filtering them out, and getting clarity,
we can see there are different dynamics in how they run different patterns in our lives,
how the Saboteur or really the Villain through our anger goes and treats people
routinely, how our Victim typically plays out, how our Princess sets up expectations of
                                                                                                                           7/10

other people and how they should treat us, how our Victim and our Judge then react,
how our Villain and our Saboteur sabotage those relationships, not because the person
really mistreated us, but because due to our Princess filter we react as if they did. These
is how the archetypes are woven, this is how they set up patterns of behavior within us.
Within these six there are so many plays between one to the other, and the more we can
break them down, the more that we can discern the subtleties of each and how we go
from one to the other, to the other, to the other. Often in the reaction we can go so fast
from one to the other, that by the time we have an emotional reaction we don’t notice
the number of agreements we step through. Then this is what I want you to look for.
And I want you to scrutinize these behaviors, these behavior patterns that you have and
break them apart into these archetype characters. And you can look at them both in our
dialogue that is in our head, in the stories we tell in our mind, and also in our outward
behavior and in how we interact with people or the world – our archetype characters
come out in both places.

Something else to notice: sometimes they come so fast, but also sometimes they come
together. One of my favorites is the Mother character. And what I am thinking of is the
mother that is unappreciated and feels like her kids aren’t giving her the respect that she
deserves cause she’s worked so hard for them and she only asks so much from them,
and she asks why don’t they do this for her. Well, in two or three sentences we can see
that there’s a number of archetype characters in there. She could say: “I work so hard
for you kids, don’t you see what I do for you? I just ask for this one thing.” You can even
narrow it down and say: “I just ask for this one thing.” But what’s in there? What’s in
there is a Victim that feels abandoned and betrayed, a Princess that says “I’m entitled to
this, because I worked so hard, I earned it, you owe this to me,” there’s the Judge that
says “You are wrong for not giving me this,” there’s the Hero that’s worked so hard to
get attention, to get approval, to get reward,” there’s the Prostitute that’s worked so
hard, that sacrifices so much of her life for someone else, and then there is the Villain
that’s imposing and kind of inflicting the anger or resentment, or actually more like
guilt into this other person, as punishment, and more guilt and punishment until this
person doesn’t want to be punished any more and they acquiesce. In one line we can
have all six: six different story lines, six different attitudes within that portrayal of that
character of the Mother.

The reason that I break down our different aspects into these different characters is
because in one sentence we can have six different agreements from six different
archetypes. Then if we are to dissolve this kind of behavior we’ve got to dissolve all six
agreements, which is why I break this up into different archetype characters. It’s hard to
change one behavior that’s got six different directions to it. But if we can see the
individual directions, now instead of changing one whole group, we can start by
changing just one at a time. A lot of times we don’t have a personal power to change
these huge behaviors or huge reactions, but we can have the power to change small
agreements. And if we change a lot of small agreements, we can change huge behaviors.
What I want you to specifically do in this assignment is in your stories that you’ve been
writing in a third person, you’re going to write what the archetype characters are saying

                                                                                                                           8/10

and doing. In the beginning we wrote as “she said”, “he thought”, “he felt”, “he said this

10 Archetypes

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community

Archetypes lesson audio

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Archetype lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times.

2. Spend time journal writing your thoughts, emotions and behaviors. Identify
where the archetype characters are active in your life and write about what they
are doing. This is an extension of the writing about characters. The difference here is
that you want to look out for these 6 specific characters. You may or not have all of
them. You also may have their characteristics interspersed into your other characters.

3. By writing you are practicing an observer perspective of these patterns of
emotion, thoughts, and behaviors.

Some notes
The journal writing is about what these Archetype characters are up to in your life. Your
third person writing that morphed to be writing about characters, now includes writing
about these Archetype characters as well.

You may find that you had some or most of them figured out already. Or, you may find
that you saw different parts of these behaviors/attitudes in different characters of yours.
For example, what you saw as just the Victim before, you might now see the entitlement
as a separate Princess component.

What looked like a forest before you started, you can get clarity and see the individual
trees during the characters exercise. In this exercise, you are getting more specific and

                                                                                                                                         1/6

can see more detail. Not all the trees look alike. The Douglas fir is not the Aspen, which
is different from the Oak, and that is different from the Ponderosa pine.

This is easier if you spent time working the characters exercise. The characters
exercise is easier if you spent time writing third person. The writing third person is
easier is you did work on noticing your Attention in the third session. Each step of the
way you are building more clarity.

If you haven’t been doing these exercises, identifying these characters may not be
obvious to you.

It is always easier to see them a day later, or an hour later. With practice the delay in
waking up to observe them gets shorter and shorter. When the delay gets short enough
you can finally be the observer of them while they are happening in your thoughts,
emotions, and behaviors.

Because you see them in real time doesn’t mean that you can change what they are
doing right then. But you are getting close. If they don’t change in that moment, it is
because there is still emotion to release, and power of faith to recover from remaining
beliefs. With a bit more personal power, less emotional attachment, and a bit more
observer perspective you will be able to choose differently.

Resistance to change
At this point you might be one of those people that is still listening to the audios,
watching the videos, but haven’t done any writing yet. You are still getting your mind
around all this information. It might feel daunting just to realize some of what is being
presented. It can also feel daunting to dismantle some of these beliefs and characters.
Because of that, you are listening and learning, and not doing much action yet. That is
fine. A number of people have approached this process this way.

A part of your mind wants to make sure that this makes sense. It want’s to see where
all this goes to make sure it understand the journey before getting on the road.

It think there may be a belief in some people that “IF I start, then I have to
finish.” Because of this belief some people are very careful about what they start. This
might be a belief drilled into you by your parents over years. You don’t want to end up
down the road too far and find out that you don’t want to be there. You also don’t want
to end up in a cult or something like that. In the meantime, your curiosity is still strong,
and so you keep listening.  All of these approaches are fine. At a certain point a part of
your integrity will jump in and decide that you are going to take the journey, or not.

Different people have different beliefs, and characters deciding their choices, and they
are all fine. Those beliefs, and those sub-personalities were developed early in your life
for very good reasons of adaptions to a weird and chaotic world. Those characters and
belief systems guided you in the best way that you knew how.

                                                                                                                                  2/6

You very well want to make sure that the upgrade program of Belief System 2.0, is
going to be better before you start dissolving Belief System 1.0.

It’s all okay. Everyone has their own process and time line to make sure it works for
them.

In the meantime, the Judge and Victim might very well tell you that you are going too
slow, or not doing enough. I assure you that they don’t know this process very well.
They don’t have wisdom, patience, compassion, or a sense of what you need to feel
emotionally safe to dismantle some of these stories. Just the same, they are full of
opinions about a process they have no experience with. They say what they say about
everything. If you were going faster than anyone had ever gone, the would still say you
are going too slow. That’s just the myopic story they are stuck in.

Consider being a little bit patient with your Judge and Victim characters. It is kind of
difficult process for them to realize that the don’t know that much.

In the Self Mastery II series, you get tools to address them more directly, and the layers
of beliefs they operate by.

Common questions

What if I don't see one or more of these characters?
It simply means that you don’t see them. You might not see them because they are not
very strong in you. Or you might not see them because you are so deeply immersed in
them as your identity, that you can’t see what you are merged with.

In either case, no worries. As you continue the practice, and clear away some layers,
you will perceive more. I’ve had some clients not see one of their particular archetypes
for 6-12 months. Then, when they were ready, they noticed what they were doing in a
different way, and they saw it as an automatic character instead of their authentic self.

Trust the process is working for you as it should.

Can these Archetype characters be good also?
Yes, in certain ways, they were all good for you at one time. And in many ways they are
still good. However, anything good, in too strong a proportion, can be toxic.

A Pleaser/Prostitute character in it’s Integrity is loving towards other people. This is
beautiful. When it is motivated to get acceptance, because you don’t have it for your
self, then it is living in pain, and looking for water in a mirage. Nobody’s acceptance will
quench that thirst but your own.

The villain can throw out some anger. Anger is a kind of defense and a crude way to
put up a boundary. If it is the only method of boundary you have then it can be better
than none. In the past it may have been your only boundary tool.

Take your time writing how each of these Archetypes benefit you, and how each might
go too far to sabotage your happiness.

The Villain can be a protector of sorts, but can be a destroyer of relationships as well.

Finding that line in between is a balance of awareness.

Fear of being berated by the judge is certainly a motivation but it doesn’t work very
